analysis: The introduction narrows a familiar agglomeration explanation by asking why residents remain where wages and employment are weak.
Housing durability supplies an explicit price-versus-quantity mechanism before the formal model.
Geography and housing consumption are defined before the rent-distance condition; the model uses strong simplifying restrictions.
The conclusion distinguishes a predictive housing-price relationship from a causal estimate.
The introduction makes neighborhood elasticities necessary for the policy question, rather than assuming a metropolitan estimate transfers unchanged.
The construction discussion separates parcel development from intensity conditional on development.
The linked equations are accompanied by definitions of employment, residents, commuting, and the computational use of the system.
The policy comparison connects a changed geographic elasticity input to changed surplus calculations.
The motivating facts permit opposing welfare interpretations; the paper states that ambiguity before choosing a model.
The text distinguishes observed wages and employment from unobserved productivity before describing the estimation problem.
An amenity residual is defined through preferences and measured wages and rents, not observed directly as a named mechanism.
The literature discussion identifies the response margin added to earlier labor-demand analyses.
The opening separates covered tenants, landlords, and the overall rental market.
Subgroups are defined using explicit age, tenure, and local rent dimensions before interpretation.
The continuation-value cancellation is tied to a specified action comparison; it is not an unrestricted shortcut.
Utility components are introduced separately and converted into rent-equivalent units under structural estimates.
The contrast keeps central-city and metropolitan population distinct.
The institutional account explains why actual construction is endogenous before introducing planned routes as instruments.
The results section names the outcome, highway-ray unit, and long-difference versus panel designs.
The conclusion preserves the need for additional explanations of suburbanization rather than treating one estimate as a complete mechanism account.
The diagram defines lane kilometers, vehicle-kilometers traveled, and average cost before formalizing their relationship.
A preferred OLS specification is distinguished from the preferred estimation method.
Household travel and metropolitan traffic are different outcomes, supporting different parts of the mechanism discussion.
The conclusion narrows claims for road classes where instruments and boundary changes limit inference.
Preference recovery is motivated by allocation and sorting, not by a generic claim that neighborhoods matter.
The observed sorting evidence creates a reason to introduce the subsequent choice model.
The second estimation step is related explicitly to the earlier price regression, so the new equation answers an existing question.
The conclusion explains why a boundary design can remain affected by sorting in other neighborhood attributes.
Earlier adult and older-youth findings motivate a different population and observation horizon, rather than being dismissed.
Treatment assignment, controls, site indicators, weights, and family clustering are explained alongside the regression.
Age at move and exposure duration cannot be separated conclusively by this design; the mechanism discussion retains that limit.
The interpretation states which childhood ages are observed and which extrapolations remain open.
